meta.title: The Window Stays, the Third Moves
meta.summary: A CAGED window is anchored on the root, not the quality, so A minor's five windows sit exactly where A major's do and the only thing that moves is the third.

spans.text: A minor's five windows are in exactly the same five places as A major's. Not close — exactly. A window is a fret span positioned by the chord's root, and the root didn't change. What changes is only what's marked inside it.

Before any of the five gets a lesson of its own, two of them deserve to be named right now, because this chapter runs strict C-A-G-E-D order and that means it opens on the least friendly of the five. The A form of A minor is the open

Their degrees are a matter for their own lessons; hold onto the fact that you own them while the C form makes you work for the rest.
The roots themselves need no new lesson. A root has no quality — an
whether the chord around it turns out major or minor, and this pathway has no roots chapter for exactly that reason. If you want a refresher on where they all sit,
One convention before the diagrams start, and it holds for the rest of the chapter. A window diagram doesn't draw one chord you could grab. It lights every

inside the window — 7 or 8 dots here, where a hand only ever holds 4 to 6 of them at once. The window is the territory; the grip is a route through it. Which of those dots a hand can actually reach together is

spans.text: Count the dots: six against seven. That's not rounding error and it isn't the diagram being careless — it's the edge effect, and it's worth seeing exactly why it happens rather than just accepting it. The window's edges are fixed frets. A
sitting on the window's bottom fret flattens to a
that falls outside the picture entirely, and a
one fret above the window's top fret steps into it. Here it's the second case: A major's
, a fret above the window's top edge, so it never showed up in the major diagram at all. Its
lands one fret lower — inside the window — and the minor diagram gains a dot the major one never had.
"The same picture with one dot moved" is false of the window — the dot counts usually differ. It's true of the grip:
, one finger, one fret. The window and the grip are not the same claim, and this chapter needs you to keep them separate.
